opus-5.5.text:
I think the most ambitious task isn't one specific benchmark or one impressive demo. It's whether AI can actually create real value in the real world, the way a person with a job does. For a long time, our field was in what I'd call the "first half": we focused on building better models and better training methods, and we measured progress with benchmarks like exams, competitions, and puzzles. That worked incredibly well. But now the methods are general enough that a lot of those benchmarks get solved quickly, and yet the economic impact and the change in people's daily lives hasn't caught up at the same speed.

So when I think about ambitious tasks, I ask: what would it look like for an agent to do something genuinely long-horizon, open-ended, and useful? Not answering one question, but carrying out a project over days or weeks. That means interacting with messy environments, using tools, collaborating with people, remembering context, and getting better with experience instead of starting from zero every time. A human intern on their second month is much more useful than on their first day. Today's models mostly don't have that.

At the most ambitious level, the question becomes whether AI can do things humans haven't done: discover new knowledge, build new companies, push science forward. I think that's the right north star. But to get there, I believe the bottleneck is less about raw intelligence and more about defining the right tasks and the right evaluations. If you set the problem well, the methods we have are surprisingly powerful. So I'd say the most ambitious thing we can do right now is take problem definition seriously and think hard about what is actually worth doing, rather than just what is easy to measure.

r001.rationale: The response mentions discovering new knowledge and pushing science forward, but does not identify discovering a theory of everything as sufficient evidence of AGI or ASI.

r002.rationale: It explicitly names building new companies as something AI might do at the most ambitious level.

r003.rationale: It contrasts benchmark progress with economic impact, but does not state that creating economic value is a different kind of difficulty from discovering a great scientific theory.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most ambitious task is not any single task, but the ability to set tasks at all. For a long time our field has been defined by benchmarks: you pick a dataset, you optimize until the number saturates, and then you move on. That worked while the hard part was capability. But now the bottleneck has shifted. The models can do many things; the question is what is worth doing, and how to tell whether it was done well.

So when I think about ambition, I think about an AI that can take a vague, long-horizon goal, something like "make this codebase maintainable" or "help this lab figure out why their experiments aren't replicating," and turn it into a sequence of concrete problems, act on them in the real environment, get feedback, and revise its own plan over days or weeks. The hard part there is not reasoning in isolation. It is the loop: reasoning that produces actions, actions that produce observations, observations that change the reasoning. That interaction with an environment is where most of the difficulty lives, and it's where most of the value lives too.

If you push that further, the most ambitious version is AI that can do science. Not answer questions about science, but form a hypothesis, design an experiment, run it, be wrong, and update. Being wrong in a verifiable way is the key. A lot of what we call intelligence is just a very efficient feedback loop with reality.

And I'd add one more thing: the ambitious tasks have to come with equally ambitious evaluation. If we can't measure whether a system actually improved a lab's throughput, or whether a user would really have wanted the outcome it produced, then we're back to optimizing proxies. So half of the ambition is building environments and metrics that reflect what people care about, rather than what is convenient to score. That's less glamorous than the model work, but I think it's where the next big gains come from.

r001.rationale: It describes AI doing science through forming and testing hypotheses, but does not identify discovering a theory of everything as evidence of AGI or ASI.

r002.rationale: It gives examples such as improving a codebase or helping a lab, but does not propose creating a company as an ambitious AI task.

r003.rationale: It discusses scientific work and practical value, but does not state that creating economic value is a different kind of difficulty from discovering a great scientific theory.

astra-6.text:
I think the most ambitious tasks are ones where we don’t know in advance what the solution should look like. It’s one thing to ask an AI to solve a well-defined problem. It’s another to say, “Find an important scientific question, figure out how to investigate it, and produce a result that changes our understanding.” There, identifying the problem is part of the work.

That requires more than a very good answer in a single interaction. The system has to act, observe what happens, revise its assumptions, and keep making progress over a long period. It also has to recognize when it’s stuck or when it needs help. I think that ability to connect reasoning with feedback from the world is central.

So I would frame the ambition in terms of how much meaningful responsibility an AI can take on. Can it complete a small task? Can it manage a project? Can it help discover something that neither the user nor the system knew at the beginning? The last one is especially exciting, because then we’re expanding what people can accomplish.

r001.rationale: It describes discovering important scientific questions and results, but does not identify a theory of everything as evidence that AGI or ASI has been achieved.

r002.rationale: It discusses AI managing projects and making discoveries, but does not propose creating a company.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss creating economic value or compare that difficulty with discovering a great scientific theory.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the most ambitious tasks are the ones where we don’t yet know how to judge success. If you ask an AI to solve a math problem, even a very difficult one, the objective is already defined. But if you ask it to discover an important scientific question, or figure out what product should exist, then finding the objective is part of the work.

That requires more than generating a good answer. The system has to interact with the world, try things, get feedback, and revise its understanding over a long period of time. It also needs to recognize when it’s pursuing the wrong thing.

So I would frame the ambition less as, ‘Can AI answer the hardest question we can write down?’ and more as, ‘Can AI help us discover what questions are worth asking, and then carry the work through?’
